title: Hugepage Allocation and Usage
exclusions: Measures only the default-size explicit HugeTLB pool counters exported in `/proc/meminfo`; it does not measure Transparent Huge Pages (`AnonHugePages`, `ShmemPmdMapped`, or khugepaged), per-NUMA-node placement, cgroup or process ownership, or each non-default pool under `/sys/kernel/mm/hugepages/hugepages-*`. The alert detects sustained low unreserved pool headroom, not a failed `mmap`, `shmget`, or page-fault allocation, and it cannot identify a host that has stopped sending events without a separate inventory-backed freshness control. `Hugetlb_kB` is retained as all-size context and must not be assumed equal to `HugePages_Total * Hugepagesize_kB` when multiple page sizes are active. A result is operational capacity evidence, not proof of a kernel defect, application impact, attacker activity, or regulatory compliance.
evidence: After deployment, retain the `UC-1.1.31 - Hugepage Allocation and Usage` saved-search definition and ACL, scheduler and triggered-alert history, each result row (`_time`, `host`, page counts, `Hugepagesize_kB`, `Hugetlb_kB`, derived percentages, and `reason`), the source events for the three evaluated buckets, the effective scripted-input and sourcetype configuration, the collector file hash, a same-time `/proc/meminfo` comparison, threshold approval, and dated positive/negative control outputs. These artifacts show how the documented rule operated on collected hosts; this documentation review did not create or validate them in a running Splunk deployment.

controlTest.positiveScenario: In a staging index using `sourcetype=linux:hugetlb`, add three `event_type=pool_sample collection_status=ok` events for `host=hugetlb-lab-01` in consecutive five-minute buckets. Set `HugePages_Total=100`, `HugePages_Free=15`, `HugePages_Rsvd=6`, `HugePages_Surp=0`, `Hugepagesize_kB=2048`, and `Hugetlb_kB=174080` on each event. Run the SPL with bounds that include all three samples. Expect one row with `allocated_pages=85`, `allocated_pct=85`, `unreserved_free_pages=9`, `unreserved_free_pct=9`, `sample_count=3`, and `reason=low_unreserved_headroom`.
controlTest.negativeScenario: In a separate staging interval, add three valid consecutive samples for `host=hugetlb-lab-02` with `HugePages_Total=100`, `HugePages_Free=20`, `HugePages_Rsvd=10`, `HugePages_Surp=0`, `Hugepagesize_kB=2048`, and `Hugetlb_kB=163840`; exactly 10 percent unreserved headroom must not fire because the comparison is strictly `<10`. Also add `host=hugetlb-lab-03` with only two below-threshold samples and a `host=hugetlb-lab-04 event_type=collector_error collection_status=error error_code=meminfo_unreadable` event. Expect zero rows, proving the boundary, three-sample persistence, and collector-error exclusion.

dataSources: One single-line key-value event per Linux host every 300 seconds from a locally owned read-only `/proc/meminfo` scripted collector, routed to the locally chosen `index=os` and custom `sourcetype=linux:hugetlb`. Neither the sourcetype nor its fields are supplied by Splunk or `Splunk_TA_nix`. The successful-event contract is `event_type=pool_sample`, `collection_status=ok`, and integer fields `HugePages_Total`, `HugePages_Free`, `HugePages_Rsvd`, `HugePages_Surp` (pages), `Hugepagesize_kB` (kB per default-size page), and `Hugetlb_kB` (kB consumed by HugeTLB pages of all sizes). `_time` and `host` come from Splunk input metadata.
app: A locally maintained collection app that owns the `linux:hugetlb` event contract and reads `/proc/meminfo`; a Splunk Universal Forwarder can execute the scripted input and transport its stdout. No Splunkbase app is required, and `Splunk_TA_nix` must not be credited with producing this custom sourcetype.
spl:
index=os sourcetype="linux:hugetlb" event_type="pool_sample" collection_status="ok" earliest=-20m@m latest=@m
| eval event_time=_time, HugePages_Total=tonumber(HugePages_Total), HugePages_Free=tonumber(HugePages_Free), HugePages_Rsvd=tonumber(HugePages_Rsvd), HugePages_Surp=tonumber(HugePages_Surp), Hugepagesize_kB=tonumber(Hugepagesize_kB), Hugetlb_kB=tonumber(Hugetlb_kB)
| where isnotnull(HugePages_Total) AND isnotnull(HugePages_Free) AND isnotnull(HugePages_Rsvd) AND isnotnull(HugePages_Surp) AND isnotnull(Hugepagesize_kB) AND isnotnull(Hugetlb_kB)
| where HugePages_Total>0 AND HugePages_Free>=0 AND HugePages_Free<=HugePages_Total AND HugePages_Rsvd>=0 AND HugePages_Rsvd<=HugePages_Free AND HugePages_Surp>=0 AND Hugepagesize_kB>0 AND Hugetlb_kB>=0
| bin _time span=5m
| stats latest(event_time) as sample_time latest(HugePages_Total) as HugePages_Total latest(HugePages_Free) as HugePages_Free latest(HugePages_Rsvd) as HugePages_Rsvd latest(HugePages_Surp) as HugePages_Surp latest(Hugepagesize_kB) as Hugepagesize_kB latest(Hugetlb_kB) as Hugetlb_kB by host _time
| eval allocated_pages=HugePages_Total-HugePages_Free, unreserved_free_pages=HugePages_Free-HugePages_Rsvd, allocated_pct=round(100*allocated_pages/HugePages_Total,2), unreserved_free_pct=round(100*unreserved_free_pages/HugePages_Total,2), allocated_default_pool_kB=allocated_pages*Hugepagesize_kB
| sort 0 host _time
| streamstats window=3 current=t count as sample_count count(eval(unreserved_free_pct<10)) as low_headroom_samples earliest(_time) as window_start latest(_time) as window_end by host
| eventstats latest(_time) as newest_bucket by host
| where _time=newest_bucket AND sample_count=3 AND low_headroom_samples=3 AND window_end-window_start<=720
| eval reason="low_unreserved_headroom"
| table _time sample_time host HugePages_Total HugePages_Free HugePages_Rsvd HugePages_Surp Hugepagesize_kB Hugetlb_kB allocated_pages allocated_default_pool_kB allocated_pct unreserved_free_pages unreserved_free_pct sample_count reason
| sort 0 unreserved_free_pct host
description: Evaluates the newest default-size HugeTLB pool snapshot in each five-minute bucket and returns a host only when three closely spaced samples all have less than 10 percent unreserved headroom. It distinguishes allocated pages from pages committed by reservations and preserves the kernel's page counts and kB fields for triage.
value: HugeTLB pages are reserved kernel memory and cannot be swapped under pressure. Detecting a persistently exhausted uncommitted pool gives Linux and database teams time to compare workload demand with pool sizing before a new non-reserved allocation is denied or a service's large-page performance assumptions are broken.
implementation: Deploy the documented local scripted collector at a 300-second interval, preserve page counts separately from kB values, and verify each normalized event against the same host's `/proc/meminfo`. Schedule the search every five minutes over a 20-minute lookback and alert only after three below-10-percent samples. Treat 10 percent as a tunable starting policy, not a Linux or Splunk default, and monitor collector freshness separately.
visualization: For all valid samples, plot `unreserved_free_pct` by host with a labeled 10-percent policy line and show `allocated_pct` as secondary context. Pair the trend with a latest-state table containing the four page counters, `Hugepagesize_kB`, all-size `Hugetlb_kB`, sample time, and derived page counts. Add a separate inventory-backed stale-host panel; never coalesce a missing sample to zero or combine page counts and kB on one axis.
dataModelAcceleration: Not applicable. `linux:hugetlb` is a custom operational metric contract with no claimed CIM data-model mapping; use the raw-event SPL.

knownFalsePositives:
1. **Oracle, PostgreSQL, JVM, or DPDK planned startup** — A service may intentionally reserve most of a pre-sized HugeTLB pool during startup. Match the host, service unit, and three sample times to the approved deployment or restart record, then suppress notification for that exact host and bounded change window; keep the capacity trend visible.

2. **Approved database load or failover test** — A disaster-recovery rehearsal or benchmark can consume the standby host's unreserved pool as designed. Confirm the named test run, application allocation target, and restoration criteria. Use the test scheduler's start/end window for temporary suppression rather than a permanent threshold exception.

3. **Intentional pool reduction through `vm.nr_hugepages`** — Configuration management can lower the persistent pool while reservations remain, causing low headroom without unexpected workload growth. Correlate `HugePages_Total` with the change record and `/proc/sys/vm/nr_hugepages`; suppress only the changed host until the post-change capacity check is accepted.

4. **Workload class designed for near-full reservation** — Some dedicated hosts deliberately commit nearly the entire pool, so `<10` percent is a poor paging threshold even though the measurement is correct. Distinguish the class through the asset or service inventory, document its minimum absolute spare-page requirement, and implement a reviewed host-class threshold instead of excluding all HugeTLB alerts.

5. **Overlapping local collectors or stale field extraction after an app update** — Two scripted stanzas, a changed key name, or mixed old/new events can select a misleading latest sample. Compare `_raw`, `source`, and effective `inputs.conf` with `/proc/meminfo`. Disable the duplicate or repair the extraction and rerun controls; do not suppress a broken measurement contract.

6. **Approved HugeTLB reservation stress test** — Kernel or application engineers may deliberately reserve pages without faulting them, increasing `HugePages_Rsvd` and reducing unreserved headroom while `allocated_pct` remains modest. Confirm the test owner and command scope, retain the expected reservation curve, and apply an exact time-bound maintenance suppression.

If exceptions are required, apply a deployment-local `linux_hugetlb_exceptions.csv` only after the core calculation, keyed by exact `host` with `owner`, `reason`, `change_ticket`, `valid_from`, and `valid_until`. Reject wildcard fleet exclusions and expired rows, and retain suppressed results for capacity review. The base SPL intentionally contains no lookup so an ungoverned file cannot silently alter the documented rule.
mitreAttack: N/A (operational HugeTLB capacity monitoring; no attacker behavior is inferred)
detailedImplementation:
## Prerequisites and measurement boundary

Assign a Linux memory owner, the application owner for each HugeTLB-consuming workload, and a Splunk content owner. The Splunk platform must have an event index available to the implementing role; this record calls it `os`, but that is a local choice and must be changed in both the scripted stanza and SPL if another index is selected. A Universal Forwarder or another approved scripted-input tier must run locally on each in-scope Linux host. Reading `/proc/meminfo` normally needs no elevated privilege, so do not grant root, `CAP_IPC_LOCK`, or permission to write `vm.nr_hugepages` merely for collection.

The measurement boundary matters. Linux documents `HugePages_Total`, `HugePages_Free`, `HugePages_Rsvd`, `HugePages_Surp`, and `Hugepagesize` as counts or size information for the default-size HugeTLB pool. `HugePages_Rsvd` is committed but not yet allocated and is included among free pages; kernel reservation documentation therefore defines generally available pages as free minus reserved. `Hugetlb` is kB consumed by pages of all sizes. This UC copies it to `Hugetlb_kB` but does not use it as the denominator. It does not monitor Transparent Huge Pages and must not combine `AnonHugePages` with these pool counters.

## 1. Configure and verify the local collector

Create a locally owned app such as `$SPLUNK_HOME/etc/apps/TA_linux_hugetlb/` and place the exact reviewed script from `scriptExample` at `bin/collect_hugetlb`. The script reads the six documented `/proc/meminfo` values and emits one line. It renames only the two source values carrying kB units: `Hugepagesize` becomes `Hugepagesize_kB`, and `Hugetlb` becomes `Hugetlb_kB`. The four `HugePages_*` values remain page counts. The script emits a classified error event rather than stale or zero-filled metrics when the file is unreadable or a required field is absent or nonnumeric.

Use this app-local `local/inputs.conf` stanza:

```ini
[script://$SPLUNK_HOME/etc/apps/TA_linux_hugetlb/bin/collect_hugetlb]
interval = 300
index = os
sourcetype = linux:hugetlb
disabled = 0
```

Leave `source` at the script-path default so responders can trace the producing stanza. Splunk documents that a Universal Forwarder can run scripted inputs, stdout becomes event data, and stderr is written to `splunkd.log`. One host therefore produces 288 normal events per day at the five-minute interval, plus classified error events if collection fails.

Configure `[linux:hugetlb]` on the applicable parsing and search tiers with `SHOULD_LINEMERGE = false`, `DATETIME_CONFIG = CURRENT`, and `KV_MODE = auto`. The event intentionally contains no embedded timestamp: `_time` is ingestion time and `host` is input metadata. Automatic equals-delimited extraction supplies the documented fields at search time. Do not set index-time field extraction and do not let the script emit `host=`, because either choice creates avoidable ownership and cardinality problems.

Run the script manually as the forwarder service account. Compare its successful line with the same read of `/proc/meminfo`: all four page counts must match exactly, and the numeric values labeled `kB` must map exactly to the two `_kB` fields. Confirm one event per execution, no shell diagnostics in stdout, and no duplicate scripted stanza with `splunk btool inputs list --debug`.

## 2. Validate the field contract before alerting

Use this contract search over at least 30 minutes:

```spl
index=os sourcetype="linux:hugetlb" earliest=-30m
| eval total=tonumber(HugePages_Total), free=tonumber(HugePages_Free), reserved=tonumber(HugePages_Rsvd), surplus=tonumber(HugePages_Surp), page_kB=tonumber(Hugepagesize_kB), all_sizes_kB=tonumber(Hugetlb_kB)
| eval contract_ok=if(event_type="pool_sample" AND collection_status="ok" AND total>0 AND free>=0 AND free<=total AND reserved>=0 AND reserved<=free AND surplus>=0 AND page_kB>0 AND all_sizes_kB>=0,1,0)
| stats count as events sum(contract_ok) as valid_samples values(event_type) as event_types values(collection_status) as statuses by host
| where events!=valid_samples
```

Resolve every row. A host with `HugePages_Total=0` has no configured default pool; keep it in a separate inventory view instead of pretending that zero divided by zero is utilization. A missing `_kB` field usually means the collector or key-value extraction still emits the kernel's colon-suffixed name. `reserved>free`, `free>total`, or negative values indicate a parser/contract defect, not a condition to force through the capacity formula.

Create a separate inventory-backed freshness search comparing expected Linux hosts with the newest `pool_sample` or `collector_error`. The primary alert cannot return a host that sends no data. At a 300-second interval, investigate after two missed polls plus normal ingestion latency. Keep collector-health tickets distinct from low-headroom tickets.

## 3. Configure and understand the saved search

Save the primary SPL as `UC-1.1.31 - Hugepage Allocation and Usage`. Schedule it every five minutes with cron `*/5 * * * *`, trigger when result count is greater than zero, and use the embedded `earliest=-20m@m latest=@m` bounds. The extra lookback supplies three complete five-minute buckets despite modest arrival delay; `latest=@m` avoids evaluating a partially arrived current minute.

**Understanding this SPL:** The first two `where` clauses reject missing, nonnumeric, zero-total, and internally inconsistent samples. `bin` and `stats latest(...)` reduce retries or duplicate events to one newest sample per host and five-minute bucket; unlike the previous implementation, the search never averages pool snapshots. `allocated_pages = Total - Free` counts pages already allocated. `unreserved_free_pages = Free - Rsvd` counts pages generally available to a new non-reserved request. The `_pct` values divide page counts by `HugePages_Total`; `allocated_default_pool_kB` multiplies default-size pages by kB per page, while `Hugetlb_kB` remains a separate all-size kernel measurement.

`streamstats window=3` requires three below-threshold buckets. The 720-second span guard allows ordinary scheduler skew around a nominal ten-minute first-to-third sample but prevents three old, widely separated observations from being called continuous. The comparison is strictly `unreserved_free_pct < 10`; exactly 10.00 does not fire. Ten percent and three samples are explicit catalogue starting policies, not limits specified by Linux or Splunk. Before paging, baseline normal reservations by workload class, document either a percentage or an absolute spare-page requirement based on the application's largest expected request, and rerun boundary and persistence tests after any threshold change. Do not add `HugePages_Surp>0` as an automatic incident: surplus pages can be permitted by `nr_overcommit_hugepages` and require local policy context.

Throttle duplicate notifications for 15 minutes keyed by `host` while retaining every scheduled result. Route the alert to the Linux memory owner and consuming application owner. A returned row does not prove an allocation failed; responders must inspect the application and kernel evidence described below.

## 4. Run positive, negative, and host controls

Execute the `controlTest` scenarios in an isolated staging index with timestamps in three consecutive five-minute buckets. The positive fixture must yield one row and the exact page arithmetic documented there. The negative fixture must prove three separate boundaries: exactly 10 percent is not below 10; two low samples do not satisfy persistence; and `collector_error` is outside the metric base search. Add a recovery sequence with two low samples followed by one sample at 20 percent unreserved headroom and expect zero rows. Preserve fixture SPL, exact time bounds, and outputs as logic-review evidence.

On a non-production or change-approved production host, capture `/proc/meminfo`, the collector line, and the indexed event from the same poll. For the source-of-truth check, compare with the Linux kernel interface `/proc/meminfo`; verify integer values and units without using `free`, `vmstat`, `top`, or a generic memory percentage as substitutes, because those tools do not expose this exact reservation contract. If multiple HugeTLB page sizes are configured, compare `Hugetlb_kB` with `/sys/kernel/mm/hugepages/hugepages-*` and document why it may exceed default-pool allocated pages times `Hugepagesize_kB`.

Exercise an approved reservation or workload startup in a lab, observe `HugePages_Rsvd` and `HugePages_Free`, and confirm that the derived unreserved value follows `Free - Rsvd`. Requalify the script after kernel, base-image, shell/awk, forwarder, or field-extraction changes. This documentation review verifies source semantics and static content only; it is not runtime or SME validation.

## 5. Operationalize, troubleshoot, and retain evidence

Build the dashboard described in `visualization` from all valid samples, not only alert rows. Label counts as pages and sizes as kB. Keep the latest pool-state table, low-headroom alert history, and stale-host inventory visually separate. Restrict saved-search and lookup edits to the platform team; grant application owners read access to their hosts. Review baselines after workload growth, pool resizing, NUMA topology changes, and at least quarterly for critical large-page services.

The runbook should first confirm sample recency and contract validity, then compare the host's current `/proc/meminfo`. Identify which application owns reservations or allocations through its service and HugeTLB configuration; this UC cannot infer ownership. Check `journalctl -k` and application logs for contemporaneous allocation or mapping failures, but do not claim absence of a message proves success. Confirm `/proc/sys/vm/nr_hugepages` and `/proc/sys/vm/nr_overcommit_hugepages` against configuration management. Pool resizing or application restart can affect service behavior and must follow the owning team's procedure; the Splunk alert must not write kernel controls automatically.

Troubleshoot no events with `splunk btool inputs list --debug`, script execute permissions, `/proc` availability, index routing, forwarder connectivity, and `splunkd.log`. Troubleshoot null fields by inspecting `_raw` and effective `[linux:hugetlb]` search-time settings. A page count carrying `kB`, or a `_kB` field divided as though it were pages, indicates a unit-contract violation. Repeated events in one bucket with different `source` values indicate duplicate collectors. `HugePages_Total=0` means no configured default pool, not 100-percent use. A mismatch between calculated default-pool kB and `Hugetlb_kB` can be legitimate when other page sizes exist; inspect sysfs before opening a parser defect. `reserved>free` or `free>total` should be quarantined as invalid data. Fix collection or extraction and rerun controls instead of tuning the threshold around malformed events.

Apply only exact, expiring exceptions described in `knownFalsePositives`, after core calculation. Suppression should mute notification, not erase samples or freshness evidence. Retain the saved-search export, dispatch records, result and source rows, collector hash and effective configuration, host comparison, test outputs, threshold approval, and exception records under the organization's operational evidence policy.
grandmaExplanation: We watch a special pool of large memory blocks that some demanding programs reserve for speed. If too little remains available for new requests over several checks, the team can investigate before another program is unable to get what it expects.
